newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Pressure remains on S.African interest rates-Stals.
newsitem.headline: Pressure remains on S.African interest rates-Stals.

text.p: South African interest rates remained under upward pressure with the overall deficit on the balance of payments effectively draining liquidity from domestic markets, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday.
Monetary authorities had to rely heavily on market forces to restore equilibrium, which could require higher interest rates, he told the central bank's annual meeting.

"A rise in interest rates at this stage, which forms one of the crucial elements in the market adjustment process, is widely regarded as unacceptable because of its adverse effect on domestic spending," he said.
"This limited view, however, disregards the even more disastrous consequences for the economy of not correcting a non-sustainable deficit in the overall balance of payments."
Stals said growth in money supply was "unacceptably high" and the expansion in credit was leading the country towards an untenable debt position.

"This dangerous prospect holds a serious warning for the banking sector to apply greater caution in their lending operations. It also dictates the need to continue with a restrictive overall monetary policy," he said.
South Africa's accumulated household debt had risen to more than 66 percent of personal disposable income, casting some doubt on the quality of the loan book of banking institutions.
For monetary policy purposes it was "of the utmost importance" that government fiscal deficit and dissaving be reduced further.

Stals said South Africa's inflation rate had fallen dramatically during the past few years and was likely to stay below 10 percent in 1996, but cautioned that high interest rates would need to be maintained to keep price pressures in check.
"The choice for monetary policy...is not only between higher or lower interest rates but rather between high interest rates now or high inflation in the future," he said.
Commenting on the fall in the rand which lost 20 percent of its value on a trade-weighted basis between mid-February and mid-August, Stals said the currency was now clearly undervalued.
"The exchange rate of the rand...now surely does not reflect the true economic potential of the country," he said.
South Africa was currently enjoying the fourth year of an economic upswing but Stals said there were clear signals of a cyclical slowdown in the rate of growth.

"Although the rate of expansion in the country's gross domestic product is still set on course to achieve about 3.0 percent growth for 1996, the main impetus for growth is now being provided by a recovery in the agricultural sector," he said.
By contrast the real value added by the manufacturing sector declined by about one percent during the first half of 1996.
Stals said a significantly better economic performance was needed to dent unemployment.
In 1995, when GDP grew by 3.3 percent, total employment in the formal non-agriculture sector rose by only 0.6 percent.
Stals said the Reserve Bank had taken steps to insure liquidity during recent foreign-exchange volatility.
This had resulted in an increase in the bank's net oversold foreign exchange position which had declined to only $8.1 billion at the end of February 1996.

"This net oversold position has, however, increased again to over $15 billion as the bank intervened in the forward foreign exchange market at the sliding exchange rate, mainly to enable importers to cover future commitments and make use of available foreign financing facilities," he said.

The central bank would continue to provide some assistance to the market by selling foreign currency from the official reserves, supplemented by available foreign credit facilities if necessary, Stals said.
The bank would also support the money market, assisting banks to bridge "the period of transition to more stable conditions".
Stals noted that the need for a downward adjustment in the rate of expansion in total economic activity would be reduced considerably if more long-term foreign investment was attracted.
The effective implementation of the government's macro-economic strategy could help considerably in this respect, he said.
